# Māyā the Asura's Yoga Theory — Kathāsaritsāgara's Explicit Doctrinal Passage

## A Demon Architect Explains Body-Recovery in Sanskrit Verse

Among the many subnarratives embedded in Somadeva's eleventh-century *Kathāsaritsāgara*, one passage stands out for its *unusual doctrinal-explicitness*. The character speaking is Māyā — the great *asura* (titan, anti-god) architect, the cosmic-engineering figure of Indic mythology who is credited with building palaces for the demonic forces and who occupies a complicated theological position between *opponent of the gods* and *master of certain operative-cosmic technologies* the gods lack.

In the passage White discusses, Māyā explains *the yoga theory of body-recovery* — the technical-operational doctrine of how a being whose body has been destroyed can *return* to embodiment through yogic procedure. The passage is unusual because it is *doctrinally-articulate*: Māyā delivers an explicit theoretical articulation, not just a dramatic narrative. The passage compresses a substantial *yogic body-cosmology* into a few stanzas, with operational-specificity that recovers the medieval Sanskrit yogic-theoretical-language.[^1]

The presence of this passage *in the Kathāsaritsāgara* — a story-collection rather than a doctrinal-philosophical text — is itself evidentially significant. It tells us that medieval Sanskrit *narrative* tradition could carry *doctrinal* content with unusual specificity when the narrative required it. Somadeva is not writing a philosophical treatise; he is writing a story-collection. But when a character needs to explain yogic body-recovery doctrine, the doctrinal vocabulary is *available* and *deployable* in compressed-clear form.

## What the Passage Articulates

The Māyā passage articulates several connected propositions about yogic body-recovery.

*Consciousness is separable from the body that contains it.* This is the foundational metaphysical commitment. The yogi's *citta* (consciousness) is not *identical* to his body; the body is *the current container*, and the consciousness can exist *without* this particular container under yogic conditions.

*The bondage between consciousness and body has a cause that can be loosened.* This is the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/parakaya-pravesha-art-of-entering-other-bodies-foundational-power|*bandha-kāraṇa* of Patañjali's YS 3.38]]. Māyā specifies that the bondage has a *mechanism*, that the mechanism is *understandable*, and that the understanding plus disciplined practice can produce *loosening*.

*Once loosened, the consciousness can navigate.* The unbound consciousness has *directional capacity* — it can move toward specific targets, can choose specific bodies, can travel through specific cosmic-spatial regions. Navigation is a *learnable yogic skill*.

*The consciousness can re-embody in a recovered body.* The recovery-of-a-destroyed-body theme is specific to this passage. Māyā explains that an *asura* whose body has been destroyed in battle with the gods can, under certain conditions, *return* to embodiment — sometimes by recovering the original body (if the components remain), sometimes by occupying an *alternative body*. This is parakāyapraveśa-related but with a body-recovery emphasis distinct from the standard living-host configuration.

*The procedure depends on yogic technical knowledge.* Māyā emphasizes that the recovery is *not* miraculous — it depends on *technical-procedural* yogic knowledge. The asuras can do it because they possess the *technical knowledge*. The gods may possess it too. Mortals who learn the yogic discipline can possess it. The technical-knowledge framing is doctrinally significant.[^2]

## Why an Asura Speaker Is Significant

The choice of *Māyā the asura* as the doctrinal-articulator deserves attention. Why does Somadeva put this articulation in the mouth of a demon rather than a god, a sage, or a yogi-protagonist?

The asuras in Indic mythology occupy a complex theological-cosmological position. They are *opponents of the gods* but they are *not evil-in-an-abstract-moral-sense*; they are *operatively-powerful beings* whose power-architecture is *different from* the gods'. Where the gods often operate through *direct-cosmic-authority*, the asuras operate through *operative-yogic-technique*. Māyā specifically is the *master architect* — the operative-cosmic-engineer.

Putting the yogic body-recovery doctrine in Māyā's mouth implicitly says: *this is operative-technical-knowledge, not divine-grace*. The doctrine is *available* to whoever masters the *technique*, regardless of their cosmological-moral position. The gods do not own it; the asuras have it; yogis can acquire it. The doctrine is *democratically operative* in the cosmological sense — accessible through technique-mastery, not restricted by birth-status.

This is doctrinally significant for the broader operative-yogic tradition's self-understanding. The tradition imagines its operative powers as *technique-based* rather than as *grace-conferred*. The yogi who masters the technique gains the powers, regardless of his social-cosmological position. Māyā's articulation grounds this self-understanding in cosmological-mythological narrative.[^3]

## The Passage's Evidence Value

For White's broader argument, the Māyā passage is evidentially significant because it provides *unusually explicit doctrinal articulation* of yogic body-recovery within a *narrative-source* (the Kathāsaritsāgara). Most parakāyapraveśa material in the medieval narrative tradition is *implicit* — the stories assume the doctrinal-architecture without explicating it. Māyā's passage is *explicit* — it articulates the architecture in compressed-doctrinal form.

This is the kind of source-passage that *resolves interpretive ambiguity*. If parakāyapraveśa were merely a literary-trope (Bloomfield-default), it would not require explicit doctrinal articulation. The Māyā passage is *doing doctrinal work* — explaining the underlying theory — which presumes the audience expected such theory to be available. The presumption requires that the doctrinal architecture was *real cultural-intellectual content*, not just a narrative device.

The passage also tells us that *medieval Sanskrit narrative authors* could and did write doctrinal-yogic passages with operational specificity. The Sanskrit narrative corpus is *more doctrinally-informative* than scholars have sometimes assumed. Hunting through the corpus for passages like Māyā's would significantly extend the recoverable medieval yogic-doctrinal record.[^4]

## Implementation Workflow: Hunting Doctrinal Passages in Narrative Sources

You are reading a translation of the Kathāsaritsāgara. You encounter a passage in which a character — sometimes named, sometimes anonymous — delivers a *theoretical articulation* of yogic operation, body-cosmology, or operative-tantric doctrine. Stop. This is the kind of passage that *most easily gets skimmed past* in narrative-reading mode. Read it slowly. Translate the doctrinal vocabulary against itself.

Ask: what is the *speaker-context*? Why has Somadeva put this articulation in *this* character's mouth? What does the choice of speaker tell you about the *doctrinal-political position* the articulation occupies in the cultural landscape?

Ask: what is the *operational specificity*? Does the articulation specify *what to do* (procedural) or only *what is the case* (metaphysical)? Procedural specificity is rare and high-value. Metaphysical-only articulations are more common and easier to find.

Ask: what is the *intertextual position*? Does the articulation echo, extend, contradict, or refine passages in Patañjali, in the Tantric ritual manuals, in the Mahābhārata's yogic material? Cross-referencing reveals the doctrinal-network the articulation participates in.

A month later you encounter another narrative-source doctrinal passage — perhaps in the Yogavāsiṣṭha, perhaps in a medieval *purāṇa*, perhaps in a vernacular yogi-romance. You can apply the same scan. Doctrinal articulations embedded in narrative are *evidentially-rich* and *systematically under-read*.

## The Māyā-Passage Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You read the Kathāsaritsāgara as *story-collection only* and skim past doctrinal articulations as *digressive philosophical material*. The diagnostic: you finish the collection with a sense of its narrative variety but no doctrinal-recovery yield. The corrective: slow down at doctrinal passages; treat each as a *primary source* for medieval yogic theoretical-language; read against Patañjali and the ritual manuals to triangulate.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The principal tension: the Māyā passage is one passage in an enormous compilation. Reading it as evidentially-foundational risks *over-weighting* a single passage. White's response (and the response the broader scholarly practice supports) is that *primary-source explicit articulations* are valuable *precisely because* they are rare. When a narrative source delivers an explicit doctrinal passage, that passage is doing *more evidential work per word* than the surrounding narrative material.

A second tension: the passage's *asura-speaker* framing may stylize the doctrine in ways specific to the demonological context. Are the doctrinal claims *standard yogic* doctrine, or are they an *asura-coded* variant? The mainstream-yogic versus asura-coded distinction is hard to make on textual evidence alone.

Open question: how many *other* explicit-doctrinal passages embedded in medieval Sanskrit narrative sources have been under-read or missed? A systematic philological project of mining the narrative corpus for embedded-doctrinal-articulations could substantially extend the recoverable medieval yogic-theoretical record.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

White's use of the Māyā passage as evidence-source converges with broader work on medieval Sanskrit-narrative-as-doctrinal-source (Granoff, Brockington, Penzer's editorial work on the Kathāsaritsāgara). The convergence is on the narrative corpus's doctrinal-informativeness when read carefully. The divergence is on how to weight individual passages — different scholars assign different evidential weights to specific instances.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The pattern of *doctrinal articulation embedded in narrative source* recurs across literary traditions.

- **History**: Medieval European *theological* doctrines are frequently articulated through *dramatic-narrative* sources (saints' lives, romance literature, sermons-as-narrative) rather than through *systematic-theological* treatises alone. Reading the narrative corpus for embedded doctrinal articulation is a recurring methodological move in medieval European religious-history scholarship. The cross-domain insight: *narrative literature is often a richer doctrinal source than scholastic-systematic literature* because the narrative requires the doctrine to be *operative-stated* rather than *systematically-derived*.

- **Behavioral mechanics**: Modern marketing-psychology textbooks frequently embed *operational-tactical principles* in *case-study narratives* rather than in abstract-theoretical statements. The cross-domain insight: *operative-tactical content is more legible in case-narrative form than in abstract-principle form*, and reading the case-narratives for embedded principles is a recurring analytical move.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**: The Māyā passage tells us that *medieval Sanskrit narrative authors had access to articulate yogic body-recovery doctrine and chose to deploy it in narrative when the story required*. The doctrinal-narrative integration is *fluent* — Somadeva is not stitching together story and doctrine awkwardly; he is *moving* between them with practiced ease. This suggests that the medieval Sanskrit literary tradition had *internalized* yogic doctrine to the point where narrative and doctrine were *not strictly separate registers*. The modern divide between *literary-narrative* sources and *doctrinal-systematic* sources may not map onto the medieval literary-cultural environment.

**Generative Questions**:
- What other narrative sources in the medieval Sanskrit corpus deliver comparable explicit-doctrinal articulations? Systematic cataloging would substantially expand the evidence-base.
- The Māyā passage attributes yogic operative-knowledge to an asura. What does the asura-attribution tell us about the *cosmological-moral status* of yogic operative-knowledge in medieval Indic thought?

## Connected Concepts

# Rati and the Five Arrows

## Five Arrows, and Their Names

Kāma's bow is made of flowers and everyone knows it. What almost nobody knows is that the arrows have names, and that the names are not romantic.

> He made up his mind that he would remain hidden. **His arrows are said to be harshana, rochana, mohana, shoshana and marana.** Even sages are deluded by these.[^1]

Take them in order, because the order is a progression and the progression is the point.

**Harṣaṇa** — thrilling, the pleasant one.
**Rocana** — making agreeable, causing to shine.
**Mohana** — deluding, confounding.
**Śoṣaṇa** — **drying up, withering.**
**Māraṇa** — **killing.**

Five arrows. The first two are pleasures. The third is a loss of judgement. The last two are a wasting and a death.

## Harṣaṇa to Māraṇa

The volume does not comment on the sequence and it does not have to. It is a curve, and everyone who has been in love recognises the shape.

The first two arrows describe what desire feels like from inside while it is going well. Thrill, and everything looking better than it is.

The third names the cost that is already being paid — *mohana*, the confounding, which is exactly what the volume shows happening: Brahmā and ten sages struck at once and unable to think.[^2]

And then the last two are not about the beloved at all. **Śoṣaṇa is what happens to a body that stops eating and sleeping. Māraṇa is where it ends.**

So Kāma's equipment is a five-stage account of desire that runs from pleasure to death, and it is delivered as a weapons inventory in a chapter about a wedding.

The same passage says these arrows work on *"even sages"* — which is not a boast about their potency so much as a claim about their **universality.** Nobody's training exempts them.

## The Wife Made From the Damage

And then, in the same scene, Kāma is given a wife.

Rati is born from Dakṣa's sweat — the sweat of a sage caught staring at his own sister — and Dakṣa hands her over with a formula that is technically accurate and does not bear thinking about:

> **She has been born from my body** and possesses beauty and all the qualities. Since she possesses qualities that are similar to yours, accept her as a wife.[^3]

*Qualities similar to yours.* She is described in the source scene as *"capable of confounding even sages"* — the identical claim made about the arrows.[^2]

So the god of desire is married to a woman who was condensed out of the first damage his arrows did, and who is characterised in the same words as his weapons.

**Rati is not Kāma's counterpart. She is his ammunition, personified, given to him as compensation.**

## He Doubts His Own Weapons

What Kāma does with her is the most human passage in the chapter and it is easy to miss under the ornament.

He looks at her, and he starts comparing her to his equipment. And losing.

> Looking at her eyebrows, Madana was filled with doubt. **"Vidhatri has placed these on her so that my bow can be surpassed."**[^3]

> On seeing the swift speed of her sidelong glances, **he no longer had any faith in the speed of his own weapons.**[^3]

> Her breath was naturally fragrant. On inhaling this, **Madana gave up all faith in the Malaya breeze.**[^3]

> As Kama looked at her limbs, **he forgot his own bow made out of flowers.**[^3]

Four losses of confidence in half a page. Her eyebrows beat his bow, her glances beat his arrows, her breath beats his wind, and finally he forgets the bow entirely.

The passage means it as praise of her beauty. But read it as what it says and it is a professional being outperformed by his own product.

> He was **pierced by his own traits** and was charmed and delighted with Rati.[^3]

*Pierced by his own traits.* The volume says it outright and moves on.

## Analytical Case Study — A Weapon Catalogue Inside a Love Scene

The composition of chapters 54 to 56 is worth laying out, because two entirely different registers are interleaved and nothing marks the transitions.

**Register one is an armoury.** Five named arrows with a fatal terminus. A bow. A banner marked with a fish. A makara mount. A list of who is vulnerable — *"I, Vasudeva and Sthanu Purushottama will come under your subjugation."*[^4] Aides assigned: Vasanta, and the sixty-four arts allocated to Rati as her friends.[^5]

**Register two is erotic description.** Rati's thighs like plantain trunks, her navel with its four sides of soft skin, her nails like kimśuka flowers, her hair like blue clouds, her breasts with the necklace hanging to the navel.

They alternate in one continuous passage, in one voice, and the volume treats them as the same subject.

Which they are, in this text's own terms. **Desire is a weapons system and a wedding is what it looks like when it is working.** The Purana sees no distance between the two, and that is a genuine and consistent position rather than a lapse.

What makes it uncomfortable is the third element sitting alongside them: the arrow named *māraṇa*, and the fact that this same god will be **burned to ash** for using it.[^6]

## Implementation Workflow

You are two months into something and you cannot eat properly.

Not dramatically. You just notice, standing in the kitchen at nine at night, that you have not had a meal since breakfast and did not think about it, and that you woke at four and lay there for an hour, and that you have read the same page of a document six times.

**That is śoṣaṇa**, and the tradition put it on the list.

Which is the useful thing about the five names, and the reason they are worth carrying out of a mythological chapter. Every culture has words for the first two arrows. Almost none has a **sequence** — a stated expectation that the thrill and the shine are the opening of a series that runs on through confounding, through withering, to something the tradition was willing to call killing.

Not as a warning against desire. The volume is not against it; it hands the equipment to a god and tells him to use it on everybody.

**As a map.** If you know the third arrow is *mohana*, then the moment you notice your judgement has gone is not a personal failure and not a sign that something is wrong with this one. It is the third arrow. It was always going to arrive.

And knowing the fourth and fifth are there does not prevent them. It only means that when you are standing in the kitchen at nine, you know what you are looking at, and roughly where you are in it.

## Named by Committee

One structural detail worth recording, because it is odd and the volume presents it as normal.

Kāma does not name himself and Brahmā does not name him either. **The sages do**, collectively, after Brahmā looks at them:

> Saying this, the best among gods **looked towards the faces of his own sons** and in a short while, seated himself on his seat on the lotus.[^4]

> All the sages, my sons, Marichi as the foremost, **glanced towards my face and understood my intention.** They understood other things too and gave him names.[^1]

And every name is derived from an effect he has already had on the people naming him.

**Manmatha** — *"as soon as you were born, **you churned our minds** and also that of Vidhātri."*
**Kāma** — because he can assume any form he wishes.
**Madana** — *"since you will intoxicate."*
**Darpaka** — *"since you were **insolent** when you were born."*
**Kandarpa** — the same root.[^1]

Two of the five names are about arrogance, given by men he has just made lose their composure. And *insolence* is the exact charge Brahmā will use when he curses him a page later.[^7]

**The word that convicts him is installed in his own name at his naming ceremony**, by the people who will be his victims, before he has done anything.

## What It Costs to Be the Instrument of Desire

The general shape, and it is why this page sits beside the curse page rather than inside it.

Kāma is given, in three chapters: a function, a set of weapons whose last two names are *withering* and *killing*, a wife made from the damage he caused, five names of which two mean arrogance, and a curse.

He is delighted with the wife. The volume spends more words on Rati's body than on the curse, and chapter 56 ends with him happy.

**That juxtaposition is the passage's real content and it is not commented on anywhere.** A being is sentenced to be burned alive, and the next chapter is his wedding, described lovingly, at length.

The tradition kept both. It did not resolve them, soften the curse, or shorten the wedding. Which is worth noting as a fact about how this literature works: **it will hold a sentence and a celebration side by side for sixty chapters without appearing to notice the gap** — and the burning, when it comes, will be narrated as a cosmic event rather than as the discharge of a grudge recorded in chapter 55.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support** is the arrow list itself — harṣaṇa, rocana, mohana, śoṣaṇa, māraṇa — a named five-stage progression ending in killing, supplied without comment inside a wedding narrative.

**Tension one.** Rati is *"capable of confounding even sages"* — the identical formula used of the arrows.[^2] The wife and the weapons are described in the same words, and she is born from the damage the weapons did.

**Tension two.** Kāma loses confidence in his bow, his arrows and his wind on looking at her, and is *"pierced by his own traits."* The volume presents this as praise.

**Tension three.** Two of his five names mean arrogance and are given by the men he has just confounded — and *insolence* is the charge on which he is cursed one page later.[^7]

**Tension four.** A death sentence and a wedding are placed in consecutive chapters with no acknowledgement of the sequence. The wedding is much longer.

**Open question.** The five arrows are named once here and, so far as the read portion of Volume 1 goes, **never used by name again.** Does the burning of Kāma in the Parvatī Khaṇḍa refer back to them — and specifically, does anything say which arrow he used on Śiva? Chapters 111–120 are unread and would settle whether the list is a live technical vocabulary or a single inherited flourish.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/kama-cursed-for-doing-his-job|Kāma Cursed for Doing His Job]] holds the sentence; this page holds the equipment and the wedding. **Read together they give the full shape of what the volume does to this figure** — commissioned, armed, named for arrogance by his victims, cursed, and married off in the next chapter.

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-ancestors-born-from-shame-sweat|The Ancestors Born From Shame-Sweat]] holds Rati's origin. **She and the pitṛs come out of the same instant** — his sweat and Dakṣa's, in one scene — which makes the goddess of pleasure and the objects of every funeral rite siblings of a kind. Nothing in the volume connects them.

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-six-vices|The Six Vices]] holds *kāma* as the first of the śaḍripu, the six enemies — where the same word names a thing to be defeated. **Here it names a person with a job, a wife, and a grievance.** The volume runs both without distinguishing them, and the endnote-layer taxonomy never mentions the god.

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-arithmetic-of-lingams|The Arithmetic of Lingams]] is the closest structural parallel elsewhere in the volume: a list in which killing sits uncommented among ordinary items, in the same units and the same tone.[^8] **Māraṇa in a wedding chapter is the same move in a different register.**

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/false-scarcity|False Scarcity]] (behavioral-mechanics).** The mechanism is that desire is manufactured by manipulating availability rather than by improving the object — the wanting is produced in the wanter, by conditions, and the object is largely incidental to it.

Kāma is that mechanism given a body, and the arrow-list is unusually honest about where it ends.

**Nothing in the five names refers to the beloved.** Harṣaṇa, rocana, mohana, śoṣaṇa, māraṇa are all descriptions of states induced **in the target**. The person desired does not appear in the equipment list at all — which is exactly the structure of a scarcity technique, where the object's qualities are not the operative variable.

The insight neither gives alone: the influence material stops at the point where the technique works, because that is where the operator's interest ends. **This list carries on for two more stages** — the withering and the killing — and names them as part of the same instrument rather than as unintended consequences. Which is a real addition: **a technique's full description includes what it does after it has worked**, and almost no manual of persuasion includes that section. The volume's version is not squeamish about it, and the last two arrows are the part any honest account of manufactured wanting would have to add.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/grief-work-and-creative-mourning|Grief Work and Creative Mourning]] (psychology).** The finding is that mourning is construction rather than discharge — the mourner builds a relationship to a figure who can no longer correct it, and the construction happens fast, at the moment of loss, and then persists.

Rati is that, run in advance and in reverse.

**She is constructed at the moment of the injury** — condensed out of Dakṣa's shame-sweat while the shame is still happening — and handed to the being who caused it, as compensation, before any loss has occurred. And she will become the volume's principal mourner: when Kāma is burned, Rati's lament is the pivot of the whole episode.

What the pair produces: **a figure built during an injury tends to keep the injury's shape**, and this one does with unusual literalness — the wife of the god of desire is made of the residue of the first harm his desire caused, and her defining act in the tradition is grief. Nobody designed that. It is what happens when three things are constructed in the same instant — the ancestors, the goddess, the curse — and nobody afterwards holds them together. Which is the same caution the ancestor material raises, and it appears here at the scale of a single marriage: **what is assembled during a crisis will still be shaped like the crisis long after everyone has forgotten there was one.**

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** Kāma's arrows have names, and the names are a progression: **harṣaṇa** (thrilling), **rocana** (making agreeable), **mohana** (confounding), **śoṣaṇa** (**withering**), **māraṇa** (**killing**). The first two are what desire feels like; the third is the judgement already gone; and the last two are a body that stops eating and where that ends. A five-stage map from pleasure to death, delivered as a weapons inventory **inside a wedding chapter.** And the wife he is given is **Rati, born from Dakṣa's shame-sweat** in the scene his arrows caused, described in the identical formula used of the arrows — *"capable of confounding even sages."* **She is his ammunition, personified, handed to him as compensation.** He then loses confidence in his bow, his arrows and his wind on looking at her, and is *"pierced by his own traits."* Meanwhile two of the five names his victims give him mean **arrogance** — and *insolence* is the exact charge Brahmā curses him on, one page later. **The word that convicts him was installed in his name at his naming ceremony, by the people he had just confounded, before he had done anything.**

**Generative questions.**

1. Every culture names the first two arrows and almost none names the sequence. Does having a *stated progression* change what desire does to a person, or only what they can say about it afterwards?
2. A full description of a technique includes what it does after it has worked. Which of this vault's influence material stops at the point of success, and what would the śoṣaṇa-and-māraṇa section say?
3. A death sentence and a wedding in consecutive chapters, unremarked, sixty chapters before the sentence is carried out. How much of this literature's emotional force comes from holding things together that a tidier tradition would have reconciled?

## Connected Concepts

# Sāmānya, Svaccha, and the Fixed Sthāyibhāva

## The Devotee Who Becomes Whoever He Is Sitting Next To

Here is a devotee whose practice has matured. `Rati` has arisen. By every measure the tradition applies, something real has happened.

Sit him with servants of Kṛṣṇa and he exhibits `dāsya`. Move him to the friends and he exhibits `sakhya`. Put him among those who love Kṛṣṇa as a child and `vātsalya` appears. Among the amorous devotees, `mādhurya`.

> Nevertheless, **his adherence to any one designated `bhāva` is not firmly fixed.** This type of `rati` is called `svaccha sthāyibhāva`.[^1]

`Svaccha` means **transparent** — and the edition's own chart glosses it exactly: *reflects that `rati` with which it comes in contact.*

A person with genuine devotion and no settled shape to it.

## Three Conditions, One Variable

The three-way division is unusually clean, and the variable producing it is stated outright: **what company you kept while your practice matured.**

**`Sāmānya` — general.** *A person who has never taken the association of even a single devotee firmly situated in his particular perfectional relationship* may nonetheless awaken a general `rati` when routine `bhajana` matures. It is called general *because it is devoid of the specific characteristics of `śānta`, `dāsya` and so on.*

**`Svaccha` — transparent.** *If one has associated in a routine manner with the five different types of devotees*, five different `ratis` may appear at different times, according to present company.

**Fixed.** *By the influence of associating with a devotee situated in one specific rasa, **only one type of `rati` among the five is awakened** when his `bhajana` matures.*[^2]

No association → shapeless. Diffuse association → reflective. Concentrated association → fixed.

**The devotee's eternal relationship with God is determined by who happened to be nearby.**

## Why That Is a Larger Claim Than It Sounds

Take it at face value.

The five rasas are, in this system, the fundamental fact about a soul's relation to Kṛṣṇa. They determine the eternal form one attains, the service one performs, the company one keeps forever. The whole `rāgānuga` apparatus is about following exemplars *in one's own particular mood*.

And this passage says which mood you end up with is a function of **whose company your practice matured in.**

Not a discovery of something latent. Not a `svarūpa` revealed. The mechanism given is straightforwardly causal, and it is environmental: *by the influence of associating with a devotee situated in one specific rasa, only one type is awakened.*

Which sits in real tension with the tradition's other account, where the `siddha-deha` is one's eternal identity, indicated by a teacher who perceives what is already there.

**Either the mood is discovered or it is caused, and this passage says caused.** The book does not raise the question.

## The Crystal, Two Texts Earlier

The image behind all this is already in the book, in the material on association:

> Just as **a crystal reflects the colour of objects that are brought near it**, a person's nature will be exactly in accordance with the association he keeps.[^3]

That verse is quoted in Text 4, in the sixty-second limb, as an argument for choosing company carefully. `Svaccha-rati` is the same crystal, named as a **stable condition** rather than as a warning.

So the tradition has one image doing two jobs. In the practice material it is exhortation: choose well, because you will take the colour. In the rasa material it is taxonomy: here is the person who took every colour and kept none.

## What Svaccha Is Not

Two clarifications the passage makes and a reader is likely to miss.

**It is not a defect.** `Svaccha` is one of three legitimate conditions of the `sthāyibhāva`, listed alongside the fixed five. Nothing calls it a failure, a stage to be passed, or a semblance. The `ratyābhāsa` apparatus — reflections and shadows — is a *different* instrument for a different problem, and `svaccha-rati` is not in it. **This is genuine `rati` with no settled shape**, not a counterfeit.

**And it is not the same as `sāmānya`.** The general type has no specific characteristics at all; the transparent type has all five, serially. One is undifferentiated; the other is fully differentiated and unstable.

Which is worth holding, because the natural reading — *shapeless, then reflective, then fixed, in that order* — is a developmental sequence the text does not assert. The three are presented as **outcomes of three different association histories**, in parallel, not as three stages.

## The Structural Consequence Nobody Draws

Follow the mechanism and something follows about the tradition's own advice.

The fifth supreme limb requires association that is `sajātīya` — *of the same spiritual disposition*, meaning devotees *who worship the same particular form of the Lord and who possess the same internal spiritual mood as oneself.*

But on this passage's account, **you do not have a mood until concentrated association gives you one.** So the instruction *associate with those of your own mood* is unavailable to precisely the people who most need direction — those who have not yet got one.

The circle is not vicious in practice; a beginner falls in with whoever is available and acquires that mood, which is what the passage describes. But it does mean the `sajātīya` criterion is **descriptive of the already-formed and useless to the forming**, and the book presents it as guidance for everyone.

`[n=1 OBSERVED]` on the circularity; both halves are separately stated and never set together.

## Implementation Workflow

You cannot tell which rasa is yours, and the literature seems to assume you know.

This passage is the one that says you may genuinely not have one — and gives two respectable reasons. Either your practice matured without concentrated association in any single mood, or it matured with diffuse association across several. **`Sāmānya` and `svaccha` are named conditions, not failures**, and a great many practitioners are in one of them.

Second scene, and it is the practical consequence. If mood tracks concentrated association, then **the question is not introspective but biographical.** Not *what do I feel toward Kṛṣṇa* but *whose devotion have I actually been near, sustained, over years?*

That is answerable, and it is a much better instrument than trying to detect a `svarūpa` by looking inward — which is exactly what the tradition elsewhere says cannot be done without a teacher's indication.

Third, and it is the honest caution. This mechanism cuts against the discovery framing that the `siddha-deha` material relies on. **I would not resolve that in either direction from this passage alone** — it is one paragraph in a taxonomy Text, and the `rāgānuga` material is more extensive and more heavily commented. But a practitioner who has been told their eternal mood is a thing to be revealed should know that the same book, in another Text, describes it as a thing acquired from company.

## Analytical Case Study: A Category for the People the System Does Not Serve

Ask what `svaccha-rati` is doing in a taxonomy of permanent emotions.

The five fixed types are what the rest of the Southern Division is about. Every rasa's `ālambana`, `uddīpana`, ceiling and compatibility is worked out for a devotee with **one** settled `sthāyibhāva`. The compatibility matrix in Text 25 assumes it. The `rāgānuga` practice assumes it.

`Svaccha` names the person that entire apparatus cannot process — and names them without demoting them.

Which is a genuinely creditable piece of taxonomy, and rarer than it should be. Most systems handle the case that does not fit by calling it immature, deficient or preliminary. This one gives it a name, a definition, a cause and equal standing among three conditions of the `sthāyibhāva`.

The cost is that it goes nowhere. **Nothing downstream is worked out for `svaccha` or `sāmānya` devotees** — no ceiling, no compatibility, no exemplars, no eternal form. They are named and then the book proceeds as though everyone had a fixed rasa.

So the taxonomy is honest at the point of classification and silent everywhere after it, which is the characteristic shape of a category admitted under pressure rather than built into a system.

Stated at the strength the evidence carries: one three-way division, read against what the rest of the Division assumes. `[n=1 OBSERVED]`.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support.** The three-fold division is Viśvanātha's own Sanskrit at Text 17's root, with `sāmānya` and `svaccha` defined by their association histories, and the *reflects that `rati` with which it comes in contact* gloss is the edition's own chart entry.

**Tension one, and it is the page.** Mood is here caused by association; the `siddha-deha` material has it revealed by a teacher's indication as one's eternal identity. Caused and discovered, different Texts, no cross-reference.

**Tension two.** The `sajātīya` criterion for association requires knowing one's own mood, and this passage says the mood comes from association. The instruction is unavailable to those who have not yet formed one.

**Tension three.** The whole rasa apparatus downstream assumes a fixed `sthāyibhāva`. Two of the three conditions named here do not have one, and nothing is worked out for them.

**Open question.** Can a `svaccha` devotee become fixed? The three are presented as outcomes of three association histories, which would suggest yes — concentrate the association and the mood settles. But nothing in the range read says so, and if the fixed mood is eternal identity rather than acquired shape, the answer would have to be no. The passage's own causal language points one way and the surrounding doctrine points the other.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The vault's Bryant material treats the five rasas as the relationships a devotee may have with God, and `satsaṅga` as a structural cause of transformation — both accurate, and presented as separate doctrines.

This passage **joins them**, and the join is the finding: association is not merely a cause of transformation in general, it is the cause of *which* transformation, and therefore of which of the five relationships a soul ends in.

Which changes what choosing company means. On the Bryant framing, good association accelerates a path. On this one, **association selects the path**, and the fifth supreme limb's insistence on `sajātīya`, `snigdha` and `mahattara` company stops being about efficiency and becomes about destination.

That is the same shape the ingest keeps finding: the settled doctrine names a practice's value, and this book names the mechanism, and the mechanism turns out to have consequences the doctrine does not carry.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**Taking the colour of whatever you are set beside, as a stable condition rather than a phase.** Set this against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/alcibiades-the-chameleon|Alcibiades the Chameleon]], whose subject is the man who stopped arguing and instead **became the mirror of whatever city he was in** — austere in Sparta, luxurious in Persia, brilliant in Athens — and whose page's sharpest observation is that Socrates was not fooled, because the mirroring was total and therefore visible to anyone who had seen more than one version.

`Svaccha-rati` is that condition described from the inside and without the strategic intent. Alcibiades mirrored deliberately; the `svaccha` devotee mirrors because his `rati` has no settled shape. **Same phenomenon, opposite agency.**

What the pair produces that neither yields alone. The Alcibiades case reads mirroring as a capability — a political instrument, brilliantly used, and dangerous to its user. This taxonomy reads the identical behaviour as a **structural condition produced by a particular history of exposure**, with no intent involved at all.

Which suggests a discrimination worth having wherever you meet someone who seems to become whoever they are with: **ask whether they have ever had concentrated exposure to one thing.** Alcibiades had Athens and chose to leave it. The `svaccha` devotee never had a single sustained association to be shaped by. The behaviour is the same; the cause is opposite; and only one of the two is correctable by changing the environment.

And it puts the harder question to the strategic reading. Alcibiades is usually read as choosing to mirror. **This taxonomy raises the possibility that a life of diffuse exposure produces the capability and the incapacity together** — that the man who can become anyone may be the man who was never long enough with any one thing to become something. Socrates' not being fooled is then not a detection of pretence but a recognition of a missing centre.

One handshake here rather than two. The caused-versus-discovered tension is the page's other half and it is an internal doctrinal conflict in this tradition; the vault's neighbours on essence and formation would restate it without sharpening it.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** Which of the five eternal relationships a devotee ends in is, on this passage's own account, determined by whose company their practice matured in — a causal, environmental mechanism sitting a few Texts from the doctrine that the eternal mood is revealed rather than acquired. The book states both and never puts them in a paragraph together.

**Generative questions.**
- If mood is acquired from company, is the `siddha-deha` discovered or ratified?
- `Sajātīya` association requires a mood you get from association. Who is the criterion for?
- Is the person who becomes anyone a person with a capability or a person with no concentrated history? The behaviour does not distinguish them.

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sajatiya-snigdha-mahattara-the-three-tests-for-association|Sajātīya, Snigdha, Mahattara — The Three Tests for Association]] — the criterion this mechanism makes circular for the unformed
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/svartha-and-parartha-rati|Svārtha and Parārtha Rati]] — the other division of `mukhya-rati` in the same Text
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-accretion-model-shanta-to-madhurya|The Accretion Model: Śānta to Mādhurya]] — the ranking of the five that this passage's three conditions sit beneath
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sadhaka-rupa-and-siddha-rupa-two-bodies-one-practice|Sādhaka-Rūpa and Siddha-Rūpa: Two Bodies, One Practice]] — where the mood is a teacher-indicated eternal identity rather than an acquired shape
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/ratyabhasa-pratibimba-and-chaya|Ratyābhāsa: Pratibimba and Chāyā]] — the other reflective condition, which *is* a counterfeit, and which `svaccha` is not
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/satsanga-association-shapes-the-soul|Satsaṅga: Association Shapes the Soul]] — the doctrine this passage turns from acceleration into selection

The *reflects that rati with which it comes in contact* gloss is the edition's chart.

[^3]: Same source, Text 4, limb 62, quoting *Hari-bhakti-sudhodaya* 8.51 via *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu* 1.2.229 — the crystal verse.

# The Hálma & the Aulós

## The Jump Set to Music

Of all the events in all the Greek games, only one was performed to music. The *hálma* — the péntathlon's jump — was accompanied by the *aulós* (the double-reed pipe), in practice and in competition alike, the player piping the Pythikón mode while the athlete launched himself off the takeoff board with weights swinging in his hands.[^1] That single strange fact — a jump done to music, in a sporting culture that left every other event silent — is the door into the hálma's meaning. The music was not entertainment. It was ritual, the same pipe-music that accompanied the cutting of the sacrificial victim's throat, here joined to the leap.

## What This Actually Is: The Mysterious Jump and Its Pipe

The exact nature of the *hálma* is, the source admits, "somewhat mysterious."[^2] It was likely a *standing* jump without a run-up, but the record of Pháyllos of Krótōn jumping five feet *beyond* the fifty-foot pit suggests it may have been more like a *triple jump* — three jumps in succession — since no single standing leap could clear fifty-five feet.[^2] (The phrase "beyond the *skámma*," beyond the dug pit, became proverbial for "beyond measure.") The athletes started from a takeoff board called a *batḗr* ("that which is trodden upon") and marked their best jumps with a *sēmeion*, as in the discus.[^3]

They also jumped holding *haltḗres* — the jumping-weights. Swung forward ahead of the jumper, the weights "add distance to a standing jump," a fact confirmed by modern experiment; Aristotélēs himself noted that "pentathletes who hold the *haltḗres* jump further than those who do not."[^4] The weights also helped ensure a clean landing, which was required for the jump to count.

The truly distinctive feature is the music. The *hálma* "was the only event in all *agōnes* to have a musical accompaniment in Classical antiquity": the *aulós* accompanied both practice and competition.[^1] The Pythikón mode was always played for it, "created to celebrate Apóllōn's victory in boxing over Árēs at Olympia."[^5] And the source draws the deep connection: the *aulós* also accompanied boxing in older times, and it "always accompanied the animal sacrifice" — it was, like the *ololyge* (the women's ritual ululation at the moment the victim's throat was cut), "an essential part of the ritual."[^1]

## The Internal Logic: Music as the Mark of the Sacred Act

The hálma's logic turns on *why music*. Every other contest ran in silence; the jump alone was piped. The answer the source gives is ritual: the *aulós* was the sound of *sacrifice*. It accompanied the killing of the animal victim, sounding at the instant of the cut alongside the women's ritual cry. So when the same pipe-music sounds over the jump, it marks the leap as a *sacrificial act* — the athlete's effort framed by the music of the offering, the jump performed inside the acoustic signature of the rite. The music is the audible boundary of sacred time: where the *aulós* plays, the ordinary world is suspended and the ritual is underway.

There is a further, conjectural layer. The Pythikón mode was created for Apóllōn's *boxing* victory over Árēs, and the *aulós* accompanied boxing in deeper antiquity; since the ancient funeral games had no jump contest, the source raises the possibility that "at some point in the genesis of the péntathlon, the hálma replaced a boxing contest" — which would explain why the jump inherited boxing's music.[^5] The source flags this as "highly conjectural," and it should be held that way. But even without the boxing-replacement hypothesis, the core point stands: the hálma is the event the sacred pipe singled out, the leap performed to the music of the offering.

## What This Organizes (Synergies & Handshakes)

The hálma is one of the five events of the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-pentathlon|péntathlon]], found only there. It shares its swinging weights with the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-palaistra-implements|palaístra implements]] — the *haltḗres* that were "specifically created for the hálma" but used across the gym for strength and conditioning. Through the *aulós*, it connects to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/athletics-as-blood-sacrifice|athletics as blood sacrifice]]: the jump piped with the music of the animal-offering is a concrete instance of the larger thesis that Greek athletics *was* sacrifice, the sacred pipe marking the leap as a ritual act rather than a sporting one.

## Analytical Case Study: The Pipe Over the Pit

Picture the scene the sources reconstruct: an athlete on the *batḗr*, weights in hand, and beside him a piper playing the Pythikón mode — the same mode, the same instrument, that elsewhere sounded at the moment a sacrificial animal's throat was opened.[^1] No other event had this. The runners ran in silence; the wrestlers grappled in silence; the discus flew in silence. Only the jumper leapt to music, and the music was the music of the kill.

Read the contrast and the meaning surfaces. If the *aulós* were merely a metronome or a crowd-pleaser, it would have accompanied every event, or the most spectacular ones. It accompanied the *jump* specifically, and it was specifically the *sacrificial* pipe. The likeliest reading is that the hálma carried a ritual charge the other péntathlon events did not — that the leap, framed by the offering's music, *was* a kind of offering, the athlete's body launched into the air inside the acoustic space of the rite. The boxing-replacement hypothesis (the jump inheriting the Pythikón mode from a displaced boxing contest) is one possible explanation for the specific *mode*; but the deeper fact it points at — that the hálma alone was wrapped in the sound of sacrifice — does not depend on it. The case shows how a single anomalous detail (one event, music; all others, silence) can open onto the whole interpretive frame: in a sporting culture that read athletics as sacrifice, the event that kept the sacrificial pipe is the one where the ritual reading is hardest to wave away.

## Implementation Workflow: Leaping to the Sacred Pipe

You stand on the *batḗr* with the weights in your hands, and the first thing to learn is the counterintuitive physics: the swing of the *haltḗres* forward, ahead of the leap, *adds* distance to a standing jump — Aristotélēs saw it, and modern experiment confirms it.[^4] You time the forward swing to the launch, the weights pulling your mass outward; and you stick the landing clean, because a sloppy landing voids the jump. The mechanics are a coordinated whole-body explosion, augmented by the swung weight and disciplined by the requirement of a controlled finish.

But take the hálma's deeper teaching: it was performed to the music of sacrifice. The transferable discipline is to recognise that *some efforts are framed as sacred and some are not, and the framing changes the act*. The Greeks did not pipe every event; they piped the one they wrapped in the offering's sound. When you mark a particular effort with the equivalent of the sacred pipe — a ritual that says *this leap is an offering, not just a jump* — you change what the act means and how you bring yourself to it. The music over the pit is the lesson: the same physical leap is a sporting attempt or a sacrificial act depending on whether you have wrapped it in the sound of the sacred, and the wrapping is a choice you make before you launch.

## The Hálma Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

The first failure is *the unaugmented leap* — jumping without the swung weights, or mistiming them, and losing the distance they add. The sign is the jumper who relies on raw spring alone when the tradition's whole technical insight is that the forward-swung *haltḗres* extend the leap; he is leaving measurable distance unclaimed by ignoring the implement built for exactly this.

The second failure is *deafness to the sacred frame* — performing the leap as mere athletics and missing that it was the one event wrapped in the music of the offering. The sign is the flattening that hears the *aulós* as accompaniment rather than ritual, that treats the hálma as just-a-jump and so misses why, alone among all the contests, it was set to the sacrificial pipe. The music was the mark of the sacred act; to ignore it is to miss what made the jump more than a jump.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The factual core is attested but genuinely uncertain at the edges: the hálma's exact form (standing jump vs. triple jump) is unresolved, hung on the single datum of Pháyllos' fifty-five-foot leap; the *haltḗres*' distance-adding effect is confirmed by Aristotélēs (*On the Progression of Animals*) and modern experiment; the *aulós* accompaniment and the Pythikón mode are attested (Pausanias). The boxing-replacement hypothesis is explicitly flagged by the source as "highly conjectural" and should be held as a possibility, not a finding.[^5] The ritual reading of the music (the *aulós* as the sound of sacrifice, hence the jump as sacrificial act) is the source's interpretive synthesis built on the documented fact that the pipe accompanied animal sacrifice — strong as inference, but inference. The perennialist-vs-critical-historical tension applies as elsewhere. Held, not resolved. Sanctus Arya trust flag applies.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The source is careful here, explicitly tagging its most speculative move (the boxing-replacement origin of the jump's music) as conjectural — a model of the honesty the trust-flag calls for, distinguishing the documented (the *aulós* accompanied the hálma and sacrifice alike) from the speculative (the jump displaced a boxing contest). The productive convergence is between the *technical* and the *ritual* readings: the same event yields a hard, testable fact (swung weights add jump distance) and a soft, interpretive meaning (the leap as offering), and the source holds both without letting the ritual reading swallow the mechanics or the mechanics dissolve the ritual. The most generative open question is the one the source leaves open — *why this event and no other?* — which the page treats as a genuine puzzle pointing toward the sacrificial frame rather than a settled answer.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

In plain terms: the hálma is *the one act wrapped in the music of the sacred, set apart from all the others by ritual sound* — which psychology meets in the way ritual framing transforms the meaning of an act, and creative practice meets in the role of imposed accompaniment and constraint in shaping performance.

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/sacred-space-time-magician-ritual-containment|Sacred Space-Time: Ritual Containment]] — the *aulós* over the jump is the audible boundary of sacred time, the sound that says *the ordinary is suspended; the ritual is underway*. This rhymes directly with the psychology of ritual containment: the marked-off space-time in which an act carries a charge it would not carry outside the frame. The hálma makes the boundary *acoustic* — the pipe is the wall of the sacred container — and sharpens the insight that the same physical act (a jump) becomes a different *kind* of act (an offering) once it is enclosed in ritual sound. The frame does not change the leap's physics; it changes its meaning, and for the Greeks the meaning was the point.
- **Creative-practice**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/constraint-based-creativity|Constraint-Based Creativity]] — the hálma was performed *to* a fixed musical mode, the Pythikón, an imposed accompaniment that shaped the rhythm of the leap. Both turn on the same move: an external constraint (the music) does not hinder the performance but structures and elevates it, the way a fixed form channels creative work. What the hálma adds is the sacred dimension of the constraint — the imposed mode was not an arbitrary limit but a *ritual* one, suggesting that the most powerful constraints are those that carry meaning, that frame the act as belonging to something larger than itself, the way the sacrificial pipe made the jump an offering rather than merely a measured leap.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**
If the hálma is right, then in a sporting culture of total silence, the Greeks chose to wrap one event — and only one — in the music of sacrifice, and that choice tells us the jump was never merely a jump. The sharp implication is that ritual sound *makes* the sacred act: the same leap, performed in silence, would be sport, but performed to the sacrificial pipe it becomes an offering. The Greeks understood that the frame is not decoration around the act but constitutive of what the act *is*. The uncomfortable question for any practice that has stripped away its ritual sound — its sacred frame, its marking-off of certain efforts as offerings — is whether it has quietly converted everything into mere measurement, all leaps done in silence, with nothing left that the pipe once made holy.

**Generative Questions**
- The hálma alone was set to music, and the music was the sound of sacrifice. What in your own practice deserves to be wrapped in the equivalent of the sacred pipe — marked as an offering rather than just an attempt?
- The swung weights *added* distance to the leap — the implement extended the body's reach. Where are you leaping without the *haltḗres*, refusing the tool that would carry you further because you trust only raw spring?
- The Greeks performed in silence except here. What would change if you imposed a deliberate "music" — a fixed, meaningful constraint — on the one effort you most want to elevate from sport into offering?

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-pentathlon|The Péntathlon]] — the event the hálma belongs to
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-palaistra-implements|The Palaístra Implements]] — the *haltḗres* the hálma was the origin-use of
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/athletics-as-blood-sacrifice|Athletics as Blood Sacrifice]] — the sacrificial frame the *aulós* marks
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-diskos-and-the-solar-cakra|The Dískos & the Solar Cakra]] — the péntathlon throwing-event using the same marker-peg
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/pygmakhia-greek-boxing|Pygmakhía: Greek Boxing]] — the sport whose Apollonian music the jump may have inherited
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/waryoga-and-nath-alchemy-hub|WarYoga Tradition Hub]] — the Greek-limb events

Sanctus Arya trust flag applies.
[^2]: Billinge, *Palaístra*, lines 3329–3331 — the jump's nature "somewhat mysterious," likely a standing jump but Pháyllos of Krótōn's leap five feet beyond the fifty-foot pit suggests a triple jump; "beyond the *skámma*" as proverbial for "beyond measure."
[^3]: Billinge, *Palaístra*, line 3335 — the *batḗr* takeoff board ("that which is trodden upon"); the *sēmeion* marking best jumps.
[^4]: Billinge, *Palaístra*, line 3335 — the *haltḗres* swung forward add distance to a standing jump (modern experiment); Aristotélēs, *On the Progression of Animals* 705a: "Pentathletes who hold the *haltḗres* jump further than those who do not"; the weights also ensured the clean landing required to qualify.
[^5]: Billinge, *Palaístra*, lines 3339–3343 — the Pythikón mode "created to celebrate Apóllōn's victory in boxing over Árēs at Olympia" (Pausanias, *Description of Greece* 5.7.10); the *aulós* accompanied boxing in deeper antiquity; the "highly conjectural" hálma-replaced-a-boxing-contest hypothesis.
